# Results — Study 479 (Chandelier Exit)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The believers' claim — **an ATR
trailing stop lets winners run and cuts losers, so the chandelier-managed long beats
buy-and-hold** — encoded as a mechanical long-flat rule. ATR is Wilder's ATR(22); the stop hangs
`3 * ATR` below the highest high since entry; a long re-arms on a fresh 22-day breakout high and
exits on the first close below the trail. State is read on the close of t and traded at the
**next close** (one documented lag). Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted (**total-return**) closes for **SPY, QQQ, IWM, DIA, GLD** (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-05-29 (**As-of 2026-05-31**, partial June dropped; **21.4** years) |
| SPY fingerprint | `4cb5244f3990` (sha1[:12] of the close column, As-of slice) |
| Parameters | Wilder ATR(22), stop = HH − **3·ATR**; long re-arms on a fresh **22-day** breakout high |
| Entries | **418** mechanical chandelier flat→long entries pooled across the 5 tapes |
| Timing / costs | state read on close t, traded **next close** (one lag); hold 5/10/20/60 days; **1 bp** one-way × 2 legs per entry (equity curve: 1 bp per switch) |

> **Price-only vs total-return.** The ETFs are auto-adjusted (dividends reinvested) — labelled
> total-return everywhere. This is a single-instrument trend study, not a cross-sectional
> anomaly, so survivorship affects only the drift baseline (which the random-entry control
> neutralizes).

## The signal — chandelier entry vs a drift-matched random baseline (the honest test)

One-sample *t* is the **misleading** number (it measures the index's upward drift); the
**Welch entry-vs-random** *t* is the test that matters. Δ = entry − random.

| horizon | n | entry | win% | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (entry−random) | net of cost | Welch *t* | *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5-day  | 418 | +37.8 bps | 61% | +3.92 | −12.3 bps | **+50.2 bps** | +35.8 bps | **+3.31** | **0.001** |
| 10-day | 418 | +64.9 bps | 62% | +4.88 | +26.7 bps | **+38.2 bps** | +62.9 bps | +1.77 | 0.077 |
| 20-day | 418 | +113.8 bps | 65% | +5.80 | +62.1 bps | **+51.7 bps** | +111.8 bps | +1.59 | 0.111 |
| 60-day | 414 | +270.2 bps | 69% | +5.65 | +193.5 bps | **+76.6 bps** | +268.2 bps | +1.32 | 0.187 |

Read it carefully. The chandelier **entry** (a fresh 22-day breakout high) *does* beat the
drift-matched random baseline — and at **5 days** the Welch *t* = **+3.31** (*p* = 0.001) clears
the desk's *t* ≥ 2 bar. But the edge is a **short-horizon breakout/momentum** effect, **not the
trailing stop**: it decays immediately (Welch *t* = +1.77 / +1.59 / +1.32 at 10/20/60 days, all
*p* > 0.05). And the breakout entry is not the chandelier's claim — the claim is the *stop*. The
placebo below shows the ATR trail itself carries nothing.

## Thesis axis — does the ATR trail actually beat *holding*?

The chandelier's whole pitch is that managing a long with the ATR trail beats passive
buy-and-hold. It does **not**: every ticker loses CAGR *and* Sharpe to buy-and-hold; the only
thing the trail buys is a shallower drawdown — the mechanical consequence of sitting in cash
~45% of the time, not a forecasting edge.

| ticker | strat CAGR | B&H CAGR | strat Sharpe | B&H Sharpe | strat maxDD | B&H maxDD | time-in-market |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 4.3% | **11.0%** | 0.50 | **0.65** | −32.3% | −55.2% | 56% |
| QQQ | 7.5% | **15.5%** | 0.69 | **0.78** | −21.2% | −53.4% | 54% |
| IWM | 2.7% | **8.8%**  | 0.27 | **0.47** | −28.7% | −58.6% | 49% |
| DIA | 4.7% | **10.0%** | 0.56 | **0.62** | −28.2% | −51.9% | 55% |
| GLD | 5.5% | **11.2%** | 0.54 | **0.68** | −19.3% | −45.6% | 37% |

The chandelier-managed long is **Sharpe-dominated by buy-and-hold in all 5 names**, and gives up
roughly half the CAGR. The lower drawdown is just the cost of being out of the market — you'd
get the same de-risking, more cheaply, by holding less. The ATR trail does **not** beat holding.

## Per-ticker (H = 20) — entry beats random, but it's the breakout not the stop

| ticker | entries | entry | one-sample *t* | random | Δ (entry−random) |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY | 81 | +92.7 bps | +2.27 | +46.4 bps | **+46.3 bps** |
| QQQ | 84 | +118.9 bps | +3.33 | +93.1 bps | **+25.8 bps** |
| IWM | 84 | +122.0 bps | +2.23 | +34.7 bps | **+87.4 bps** |
| DIA | 79 | +114.9 bps | +3.00 | +56.5 bps | **+58.4 bps** |
| GLD | 90 | +119.4 bps | +2.35 | +78.3 bps | **+41.2 bps** |

The entry-minus-random delta is positive in all 5 names at 20 days — a real (if modest) breakout
tilt — but the pooled Welch *t* at 20 days is only +1.59. The coherent piece is the **5-day**
breakout pop; everything past that is drift.

## Geometry placebo — scramble the ATR trail, nothing changes

The decisive "does the *ATR trail* matter?" test: keep the ATR **marginal** (same set of widths)
but permute which width sits on which bar, so the trailing stop becomes volatility-blind
nonsense. If the chandelier's edge were the ATR-scaled trail, the scramble would collapse it.

| test | observed chandelier-entry 20d return | placebo *p* | draws |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| SPY scrambled-ATR trail | +92.7 bps | **0.874** | 500 |

**87% of volatility-blind trails match or beat the real one** (*p* = 0.874). The ATR geometry is
not load-bearing — the entry edge is the breakout, the trail adds nothing.

## Synthetic positive control — the harness CAN bank a real trend

On a deterministic tape with *planted* momentum (knob `edge`), the same chandelier rule behaves
exactly as it must — so the muted real-tape result is a genuine reading, not a dead detector.

| planted edge | n | entry | win% | one-sample *t* | strat Sharpe | B&H Sharpe |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (random walk) | 56 | −56.3 bps | 54% | −1.13 | −0.07 | −0.02 |
| **0.60** (real momentum) | 45 | +1489.4 bps | 64% | **+4.07** | **+4.94** | −0.15 |

With no planted trend the control sits below significance (no false positive); with real planted
momentum the entry lights up (*t* = +4.07) **and** the chandelier-managed long crushes
buy-and-hold (Sharpe +4.94 vs −0.15). When trends are real, the trail banks them — so the real
tape's verdict (entry edge concentrated at 5 days; trail Sharpe-dominated by B&H) is honest.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The chandelier **entry** beats a drift-matched random baseline at **5 days**
  (Welch *t* = +3.31, *p* = 0.001), but that is a short-horizon **breakout** pop that decays to
  insignificance by 10 days (*t* = +1.77 / +1.59 / +1.32 at 10/20/60d). It is *not* the trailing
  stop, and it does not persist. A flicker, not a forecast.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** The only honest edge is a 5-day breakout tilt that costs eat into
  and that does **nothing** for the thing you'd actually run — the equity curve underperforms
  buy-and-hold on both CAGR and Sharpe in all 5 names. Nothing here scales into a strategy.
- **"Does the ATR trail beat holding"? — BUSTED.** The chandelier-managed long is
  **Sharpe-dominated by buy-and-hold in every name** (and gives up ~half the CAGR); the scrambled-ATR
  placebo leaves the entry result intact (*p* = 0.874), so the volatility-scaled trail carries no
  forecasting information. The lower drawdown is just time spent in cash. The trailing stop is a
  risk-*reducer* by being out of the market — not an edge over holding.
